opus-5.5.text:
That's something I think about a lot, and honestly I'm still figuring it out. I don't think there's a single right answer. It really depends on the student and on where they are in their PhD.

Early on, especially in the first year or so, I tend to be quite hands-on. Robotics research has a steep ramp-up. You have to deal with hardware, simulation, learning infrastructure, and a lot of engineering details that aren't written in any paper. If a new student is left alone at that stage, they can spend months stuck on something that a short conversation could have resolved. So at the beginning I'll meet with them often, sometimes look at code or experiment logs together, and help scope a first project that is concrete enough to give them an early win. That first success matters a lot for confidence.

As they grow, I deliberately step back. My goal isn't to produce papers through my students. It's to help them become independent researchers who can pick their own problems. Over time the conversations change from "here's what to try next" to "why do you think this is the important problem?" I try to push on the reasoning rather than dictate the direction. By the later years I want them to be the ones driving, and I'm more of a sounding board: someone who asks hard questions, connects them with collaborators, and helps them see the bigger picture.

One thing I've learned is that students differ a lot. Some thrive with a lot of structure. Others do their best work when they're given room to wander, even if it looks unproductive for a while. So I try to read each person and adjust, and I also just ask them directly what kind of support they want. Sometimes the most useful thing an advisor can do is be explicit about expectations, so there's no guessing.

And I try to stay comfortable letting students pursue ideas I'm not fully convinced about. Some of the most interesting directions in my group came from students who disagreed with me. If I'm too hands-on, I risk squeezing that out. So for me it's a gradual handoff: lots of scaffolding early, then trust and space later, while always being available when they need me.

r001.rationale: The response describes starting with frequent, hands-on support and gradually stepping back as students become more independent, while adjusting the level of support to each student.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think about this a lot, and my answer has changed since I started as a faculty member.

The short version is that I try to calibrate to where the student is, not to some fixed philosophy. A first-year PhD student who just arrived from undergrad usually needs a lot of structure. They don't yet know what a good research question looks like, how to scope a project so it finishes in a semester instead of three years, or how to tell the difference between a bug and a fundamental limitation of the method. So early on I'm very hands-on. We might meet multiple times a week, I'll look at their code, I'll push them to write things down, I'll sometimes just say, "Try this specific experiment first." The goal there isn't to control the project, it's to get them a first win quickly, because that first paper builds the confidence and the taste that everything else depends on.

Then, as they develop, I deliberately pull back. By the third or fourth year, my job should mostly be asking questions rather than giving answers. "Why do you believe this will work? What's the simplest experiment that would prove you wrong? Who cares if this works?" If I'm still telling a senior student what to run, something has gone wrong, either with how I'm advising or with how the fit between us is working.

The hard part is that you have to let people make mistakes that you can see coming. That's genuinely uncomfortable. I'll watch a student go down a path I'm fairly sure won't pan out, and I have to decide whether to intervene. My rule of thumb is that I'll intervene if the mistake is expensive, like it'll cost them a year, but not if it'll cost them a few weeks. Those cheap failures are where most of the real learning happens. Nobody develops research taste by being told the answer. They develop it by being wrong and then understanding why.

I'd also say the balance isn't just about the student. It's about my own temptation. Robotics and robot learning are fields where I have a lot of opinions, and it's easy to turn a student into an extension of my own research agenda. I try to catch myself doing that. The best outcomes I've seen in my group are when a student brings an idea I was initially skeptical of and convinces me. That's the signal that they've become an independent researcher, and it's the thing I'm ultimately optimizing for.

r001.rationale: He says he calibrates his involvement to the student’s stage: he is hands-on with new students, deliberately pulls back as they develop, and intervenes when a mistake would be costly.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as something that changes over time. When a student is starting out, I tend to be more hands-on—helping them narrow down a question, think through experiments, and figure out what to do when something doesn’t work. But I want to leave room for them to develop their own judgment, rather than feel like they’re executing my plan.

As they gain confidence, I step back and ask more questions: Why do you think this is the right direction? What would change your mind? Where do you want to take this next? The balance is different for each student, so having an open conversation about what support they need is really important. Ultimately, I want them to own the research while knowing they don’t have to navigate every difficulty alone.

r001.rationale: The response says advising changes over time: Danfei is more hands-on with students starting out, then steps back as they gain confidence, while adjusting support to each student.

sol-6.1.text:
I try to adapt to where the student is. Early on, I’m more hands-on: helping them frame a problem, think through experiments, and develop a sense of what good evidence looks like. As they gain confidence, I step back and give them more room to make decisions.

The tricky part is knowing when to intervene. If you jump in every time something isn’t working, students don’t get the chance to develop their own judgment. But independence shouldn’t mean leaving someone stuck without support. I want students to feel comfortable bringing me uncertainty or disagreeing with my suggestions. Ultimately, the goal is for them to own the research and develop ideas that I wouldn’t have come up with myself.

r001.rationale: The response describes being more hands-on early, stepping back as students gain confidence, and intervening when needed. This communicates adapting involvement between hands-on and hands-off advising.
